title: Names, Functions & the Rules of the Language

scenes.say: Five, or six? Take i equal to five. What does a equals i plus plus store? Half of candidates guess wrong. And some code has no right answer at all. By the end, you'll know exactly why.

Today you will do three things. Keep names apart, and see what plus plus hands back. Pick the right function with overloads, inline, and null p t r. Then tell compile errors from runtime errors, and meet undefined behavior.

Compile vs runtime errors, and undefined behavior

scenes.title: Two libraries, one name
scenes.statement: A network library and a UI library each define a function called log. Use both in one program.

example.input: net has log(), ui has log()

scenes.say: Here is the problem. Your network library has a function called log. So does your UI library. We want to call both in one program, with no clash.

scenes.head: Two cities, one Main Street
scenes.say: Think of two cities. Both have a Main Street. Say Main Street, and nobody knows which one. Add the city name, and the address is unique. A namespace is that city name, and the double colon joins it to the name.

scenes.head: Same name twice: refused
scenes.say: Here are both log functions in one file. The first prints net, the second prints ui. Same name, same parameters, same scope. The compiler refuses with a redefinition error.

scenes.head: Give each log a home
scenes.say: The fix is two namespaces. Wrap the first log in net. Wrap the second in ui. Now they are different functions. Call them by namespace, double colon, then name. That double colon is the scope resolution operator.
Your turn. Suppose a file has using namespace net and using namespace ui, then calls log with the word hi. What happens? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: using namespace net; using namespace ui; log("hi"); What happens?

scenes.head: Both in scope: ambiguous
scenes.say: Ambiguous. Both names are in scope, and the compiler won't guess. A using declaration brings in just one name, which is safer. The standard library lives in namespace s t d, and using namespace s t d in a header silently leaks every standard name into every includer.

output.text: error: call of overloaded ‘log(const char [3])’ is ambiguous

scenes.title: Same variable, two results
scenes.statement: Both ++i and i++ add one to i. Find the value each expression hands back.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. Start with i at five. Then a equals i plus plus. Then b equals plus plus i. The result is a five, b seven, i seven. Let's see why.

scenes.head: A ticket machine at the deli
scenes.say: Picture a deli ticket machine. The display is i, showing five. Post increment, i plus plus, hands you ticket five, then the display moves to six. Pre increment, plus plus i, moves the display first, then hands you the new number. Same machine, different moment.

scenes.head: Run it line by line
scenes.say: Run it. i starts at five. Line two, a equals i plus plus. The old value, five, goes to a. Then i becomes six. Line three, b equals plus plus i. i becomes seven first, and that seven goes to b.

scenes.head: How a class does it
scenes.say: Look at how a class does it. Prefix adds one and returns itself, no copy. Postfix copies the old object, adds one, and returns the copy. That copy is why loops prefer plus plus i. The extra int just marks postfix. Run it: five, seven, seven.
Your turn. i is five. Then a gets i plus plus. Then b gets i plus plus again. What is a plus b? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: i = 5; a = i++; b = i++; What is a + b?

scenes.head: a gets 5, b gets 6
scenes.say: Eleven. The first i plus plus hands out five, and i becomes six. The second hands out six, and i becomes seven. Five plus six is eleven.

scenes.title: One print for every type
scenes.statement: You want print(42) to show an int and print(3.14) to show a double, with the same name.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. You want one name, print, for ints and doubles. For example, forty two and three point one four. Each gets its own behavior.

scenes.head: A receptionist who reads
scenes.say: Think of a receptionist. One desk, one name on the door. You hand over a form, and she reads what kind it is, then sends you to the right office. The compiler is that receptionist. The form is the argument type.

scenes.head: Three prints, one name
scenes.say: Here is overloading. Three functions share the name print, taking an int, a double, and a string. Call print with forty two, and the compiler sees an int. Three point one four is a double. A string picks the third. All of it is decided at compile time.
Your turn. Same three prints, and now the call is print of the character A, in single quotes. Which one runs? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: print('A') with print(int), print(double), print(string). Which runs?

scenes.head: How the compiler ranks them
scenes.say: It prints int sixty five. The compiler ranks the candidates. Exact match wins first. A char promotes to int, which is next best. Converting to double is worse. Two equal conversions tie, and the call is ambiguous.

scenes.head: Two traps
scenes.say: Two traps. First, the return type alone does not count. These two parse functions look identical to the caller, so the second is an error. Second, a call can be ambiguous. Converting five to long or to double is equally good, so the compiler gives up.

output.text:
error: ambiguating new declaration of ‘double parse(const char*)’
error: call of overloaded ‘f(int)’ is ambiguous

scenes.head: How can they share a name?
scenes.say: How can functions share a name? The compiler mangles each one, encoding the parameter types. Print of int becomes a symbol ending in i. Print of double ends in d. The linker sees two different symbols. C cannot call these directly. A function exposed to C needs extern C.

scenes.title: Two files include one header
scenes.statement: A header defines sq. Both source files include it. Build one program from the two files.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A header defines sq, which squares a number. Two source files include that header. We want one program that links and prints twenty five and forty nine.

scenes.head: Photocopied rule sheets
scenes.say: Include is a photocopier. It pastes the header into every file. So the first file gets a copy of sq, and the second gets another. The linker then finds two sq functions, and refuses. Inline says the copies are allowed.

scenes.head: No inline: link error
scenes.say: Here is the header, with no inline. Each source file compiles fine on its own. The trouble starts at link time. The linker finds sq defined twice, and stops with multiple definition.

output.cmd: g++ a.cpp b.cpp 2>&1 | grep -oE "multiple definition of [^;]*|error: ld.*"
output.text:
multiple definition of `sq(int)'
error: ld returned 1 exit status

scenes.head: With inline: allowed
scenes.say: Add the word inline. Now identical definitions in many files are allowed, and the linker keeps one. That is the one definition rule. The program prints twenty five and forty nine.
Your turn. Inline has an older meaning too. Does the keyword force the compiler to paste the body at every call? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `inline int sq(int x)`: must the compiler paste the body at each call?

scenes.head: A hint, not a command
scenes.say: No, it is a hint. The compiler decides, with or without the keyword. When it pastes, sq of five becomes five times five, computed ahead of time. Some functions are inline for free: members defined in a class body, and constexpr functions. C plus plus seventeen adds inline variables.

chapters.title: When bugs show up, and UB

scenes.title: Which bug reaches your user?
scenes.statement: Program A has a missing semicolon. Program B divides by a number the user types. Which one can reach a user?

example.output: A never ships; B crashes at d = 0

scenes.say: Here is the problem. Program A forgets a semicolon. Program B divides ten by what the user types. Which can reach a user? Only B, and only when d is zero.

scenes.head: A timeline of mistakes
scenes.say: Think of an airport. Problems are cheapest at check in. Compile is check in: syntax and types. Link is security: a missing definition. Run is the flight: bad input crashes. Logic errors land in the wrong city: no crash, wrong answer.

scenes.head: Compile time: no program
scenes.say: A compile time error is caught before the program ever runs. A string where an int belongs. A missing semicolon. No executable is produced, so this bug can never reach a user. That is the good kind.

output.text:
error: invalid conversion from ‘const char*’ to ‘int’ [-fpermissive]
error: expected ‘,’ or ‘;’ before ‘}’ token

scenes.head: Runtime: it builds, then fails
scenes.say: A runtime error compiles without complaint, then fails while running. Say the user types two. Ten divided by two is five, fine. Now the user types zero. Ten divided by zero crashes the program. Only that one input breaks it.

scenes.head: No rules at all
scenes.say: Now the scary part. Some code has undefined behavior, or U B. Reading past the end of an array. Signed integer overflow. The standard places no requirements on what happens. Not an error. Not a guaranteed crash. Anything.

steps.cue: past the end of an array

notes.cue: past the end of an array

scenes.say: Your turn. The code writes to arr index five, but arr has only three slots. What does the standard guarantee? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: int arr[3]; arr[5] = 1; What does the standard guarantee?

scenes.head: Anything can happen
scenes.say: Nothing at all. The code may work today. It may print garbage tomorrow. It may crash on another compiler. And the optimizer may assume U B never happens, and delete your safety check.

scenes.head: Catch it with the tools
scenes.say: Compiler warnings flag simple cases, like two plus plus changes to i in one line. Sanitizers catch the rest at runtime, with the exact line. Works on my machine proves nothing. And that first line has no right answer at all.

output.cmd: g++ -fsanitize=undefined main.cpp && ./a.out 2>&1 | grep -o "runtime error: signed integer overflow"

scenes.title: Which f does the call pick?
scenes.statement: f has two versions: one takes an int, one takes a char pointer. Call it with nothing, three ways.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. f has an int version and a pointer version. We call it with zero, N U L L, and null p t r. Which runs each time?

scenes.head: Three ways to hand over nothing
scenes.say: Think of a form with a pointer box. Zero is a plain number that can slide in. NULL is a macro for zero, so also a number. Null p t r is a stamp made only for pointer boxes.

scenes.head: f(0) and f(nullptr)
scenes.say: Here are the two versions. Calling f with zero picks the int version, because zero is an int. Calling f with null p t r picks the pointer version, because null p t r converts only to pointers.
Your turn. Now call f with N U L L, on G C C. Which version runs? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: On GCC, f(NULL) with f(int) and f(char*): what happens?

scenes.head: NULL is not a pointer
scenes.say: Ambiguous. On G C C, NULL is an integer constant. It converts to an int and to a pointer equally well, so the compiler cannot choose. Auto hides the same trap. Auto of NULL is an integer. Auto of null p t r is a real pointer type.

notes.cue: Auto of null p t r

output.text: error: call of overloaded ‘f(NULL)’ is ambiguous

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is a namespace? A named box for names, so libraries can share a name. How do you reach inside? The double colon, then the name. And using namespace s t d in a header? Never. It leaks into every includer.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Plus plus i versus i plus plus? One returns the new value, one the old. With i equal five, a equals i plus plus gives five, then i is six. Which in loops? Plus plus i. No extra copy for iterators.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is overloading? One name, different parameter lists. Who picks? The compiler, at compile time, from the arguments. Return type alone? Not enough, it is an error. Any gotcha? Two equally good conversions make the call ambiguous.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Inline, old meaning? A hint to paste the body. The compiler may ignore it. Modern meaning? Defined in many files, like a header. The linker keeps one. Inline for free? Class body members and constexpr functions.
rows: a hint to paste the body; compiler decides
defined in many files; linker keeps one

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Compile time errors? The compiler rejects the code, and no program is built. Runtime errors? It builds, then fails on some input, like dividing by zero. Which do you prefer? Compile time: strong types, const, and static assert.
rows: compiler rejects it; no program built

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is undefined behavior? The standard makes no promises. Anything can happen. Examples? Out of bounds access, null dereference, signed overflow. Why dangerous? It often seems to work, and the optimizer assumes it never happens. How do you catch it? Warnings and sanitizers.
rows: out of bounds, null deref, overflow
often seems to work; optimizer assumes no UB

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Zero and NULL? Integers that can convert to pointers. NULL is a macro for zero. And null p t r? A true null pointer, with its own type. Why care? NULL can make a call ambiguous. Null p t r never does.
rows: integers that can convert to pointers

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next, all integer edge cases. LeetCode nine, palindrome number: reverse half the digits to avoid overflow. LeetCode seven, reverse integer: check overflow first. LeetCode twenty nine, divide two integers: the smallest int divided by minus one overflows.

So say this. Namespaces and overloads are resolved by the compiler. Plus plus i is new, i plus plus is old. Inline lets headers hold code. Catch errors early, and fear undefined behavior. Always write null p t r.
lines: Names and overloads: the compiler resolves them.
Fear UB. Catch errors early. Write `nullptr`.
